warmup.q: Redis's keys are split over three servers, and each key belongs to exactly one of them. A program connected only to server 1 sends one command that stores two keys at once: MSET payment:42 approved payment:43 approved. payment:42 belongs to server 2, and payment:43 to server 3. What comes back?
options: OK: server 1 passes each key on to the server it belongs to
An error that sends the program to server 2, which owns the first key
An error: the two keys belong in different places, so no single server can run the command as one step
OK, but only payment:42 is stored
warmup.why: Servers in a Redis Cluster never pass commands on. A server first checks that all the keys of one command fall in the same slot, one of 16,384 numbered groups of keys that the first section sets up. These two don't (they're in slots 9055 and 13182), so it refuses with CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot before it even looks at who owns them. A command with one key that belongs to server 2 would have got the second answer, an error called MOVED. Some cluster libraries split such an MSET into one command per slot by themselves. That works, but the two halves are no longer one step.

sections.h: Too much for one server: splitting the keys into slots
sections.html:
Let's put numbers on the café's queue. The payments program's Redis started with the payment notes from Rate limiting and idempotency keys. Then came rate limits, a cache of saved answers from slower systems, and more. Now it needs 40 GB of memory and 300,000 commands a second. Persistence and replication added a replica, a second server that copies every change, but a replica copies every key and every write. It splits neither the memory nor the work. And inside one Redis, one thread, a single path of work, runs every command, one at a time (Inside an in-memory store). So one server's speed has a ceiling. We need several primaries: servers that each own part of the keys and take the writes for them.

The simplest split lives in the program. Number the servers 0, 1 and 2. Turn each key into a number with a hash function, a formula that turns any text into a number that looks random. Then pick server hash(key) mod N: the remainder after dividing by N, the number of servers. It works until N changes. Go from 3 servers to 4, and a key stays where it was only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 3 and for 4. Over 1,000,000 keys from payment:1 to payment:1000000, 75% landed on a different server. Each of those is a lost saved answer or, worse, a payment note that seems to have vanished.

Picture a cloakroom instead, with 16,384 numbered hooks split among three attendants. A coat's ticket always picks the same hook, and a board says which attendant looks after which hooks. When a fourth attendant starts, some hooks change hands, and no coat ever moves to a different hook.

Redis Cluster works the same way. Its keys are spread over 16,384 hash slots, and a key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384. CRC16 is a 16-bit checksum, a number worked out from the key's bytes. It's cheap to compute, and its results spread evenly, so keys spread evenly over the slots. The number of slots never changes. What changes is the slot table, which says which primary owns each slot. Three primaries split it into 0-5460, 5461-10922 and 10923-16383. Adding a fourth moves 4,096 slots to it, about 1,365 from each of the others. Only the keys in those slots move: 25%, the least possible for a server that should hold a quarter of the data.

That's this lesson's model: a key hashes to a slot, and a slot belongs to one primary. Every rule that follows comes from that chain: where a command must go, which keys one command can use together, and what moves when the cluster grows or a server fails. Each server in a cluster is called a node, and every node knows the whole slot table. The nodes keep their tables in step by talking to each other on a second port, the cluster bus, at the clients' port plus 10,000. (A client is any program that talks to Redis, and a port is the number that says which program on a machine a connection is for.)

The cloakroom picture breaks in one place. An attendant can walk to another counter and fetch your coat for you. A Redis node never does. Next, we'll see what it does instead.

try.title: Ask a real cluster where keys live
steps: From the labs folder, start a three-node cluster: docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml up -d --wait. Docker runs each node in a container, a small separate machine on your computer. The nodes listen on ports 7001, 7002 and 7003, and a one-off container joined them and split the slots. Open Redis's command prompt on node 1: docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml exec node-1 redis-cli -p 7001.
CLUSTER KEYSLOT prints a key's slot. Before each one, say which node you expect to own the slot, using the three ranges above.
Read CLUSTER SHARDS: one entry per primary, with its slot range and its address. Leave the cluster running for the rest of the lesson.

code.title: at node 1's redis-cli prompt
code.html:
CLUSTER INFO
CLUSTER KEYSLOT payment:42
CLUSTER KEYSLOT payment:43
CLUSTER KEYSLOT 123456789
CLUSTER SHARDS

try.expect: CLUSTER INFO starts with cluster_state:ok and cluster_slots_assigned:16384, and further down shows cluster_known_nodes:3 and cluster_size:3. payment:42 is in slot 9055 (node 2's range) and payment:43 in 13182 (node 3's). 123456789 is in 12739. That's the test string from the cluster specification, the document that defines how a cluster works: its CRC16 is 0x31C3, which is 12,739, already below 16,384. CLUSTER SHARDS lists each primary's slots pair, such as 10923 and 16383, then its id, port 7003, ip 127.0.0.1 and role master (Redis's reports still say master for a primary). The node ids are random 40-character strings and differ on every run.

refs.title: Redis cluster specification: key distribution model

aside.title: Why slots at all, instead of a table that lists every key?
aside.html: A table of keys would be as big as the data, and it would change with every new key, so every node and every client would have to keep up with millions of entries. A fixed number of slots keeps the table small: 16,384 numbers with one owner each, and it changes only when someone moves a slot. Working out a key's slot needs no table at all, only the formula. The number is also a ceiling: a Redis Cluster can't have more than 16,384 primaries, and its documentation suggests staying around 1,000 nodes.

sections.h: A node that doesn't own the slot sends you to the one that does
sections.html:
Send GET payment:42 to node 1 with a plain client, a program that knows one address and treats it as a single Redis. The answer is an error: MOVED 9055 127.0.0.1:7002. Slot 9055 lives at 127.0.0.1:7002 (127.0.0.1 is the address a machine uses for itself, and 7002 the port), so ask there. Node 1 doesn't fetch the key for you. Cluster nodes never pass commands on, so each node only ever works on its own slots.

The simplest client follows every MOVED. With three nodes, that costs an extra round trip, a message there and an answer back, for about two keys in three. A cluster-aware client does better. When it starts, it asks any node for the whole slot table (CLUSTER SHARDS, or the older CLUSTER SLOTS) and opens a connection to every node. Then it works out each key's slot itself and sends each command straight to the owner.

A MOVED then becomes rare, and it means the table changed: a slot moved, or a replica took over from a dead primary. The client updates its table, usually by loading all of it again, because slots rarely move alone. Jedis and Lettuce, the two main Redis libraries for Java and Kotlin, both have a RedisClusterClient that works this way, and Lettuce 7 also reloads its table when it notices redirects.

Because the client does the routing, the address in a MOVED reply must work from wherever the client runs. Each node announces one address. That's behind most "the cluster works inside Docker but not from my laptop" problems: the nodes announce addresses inside Docker that the Mac can't reach. The lab's Compose file (the settings Docker uses to start the cluster) makes all three nodes share one network setup and announce 127.0.0.1 (cluster-announce-ip), so the same address works inside Docker and from the Mac.

Pipelines, batches of commands sent together, follow the same rule: a cluster client splits one pipeline into one per node. But a MULTI/EXEC transaction, a group of commands that Redis runs as one step, can't be split across nodes. That brings us to the next section's rule.

} } // Jedis 8 splits a cross-slot MSET into one MSET per slot and sends each to its node: // it succeeds, but the halves are separate commands, not one atomic step System.out.println("MSET payment:42 payment:43 -> " + cluster.mset("payment:42", "settled", "payment:43", "settled")); // the same command sent as raw MSET to one node is refused by the server try (RedisClient node2 = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("127.0.0.1", 7002).build()) { node2.mset("payment:42", "x", "payment:43", "y"); sections.h: Keys that must change together need the same slot
sections.html:
Send MSET payment:42 approved payment:43 approved, one command that stores two keys, to a node, and it refuses: CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot. The two keys live in slots 9055 and 13182, on different nodes, and no node can change keys it doesn't hold in one step. The rule covers every command that names several keys (MSET, MGET, SUNIONSTORE, RENAME), every MULTI/EXEC transaction, and every Lua script, a small program that Redis runs as one step. A script that moves money from acct:a to acct:b fails on a cluster as written. So would the lease fill from Keeping a cache honest, which checks one key and writes another, if its two keys lost their shared tag. Even two slots that happen to sit on the same node are refused, because either one could move tomorrow.

Cluster clients can hide this. In the demo, Jedis and Lettuce both accepted the cross-slot MSET by splitting it into one MSET per slot and sending each half to its node. Each half is one step; the pair isn't. A crash between them leaves one payment approved and the other not.

The fix is a hash tag. If a key contains {, then a } after it, with at least one character between them, only the part between the first { and the next } is hashed. {merchant:7}:payments and {merchant:7}:refunds both hash merchant:7, both land in slot 10890, and MSET, MULTI and scripts work on them again. In the cloakroom, it's a family asking for one hook for all their coats.

Tag by the smallest unit that must change in one step: the customer whose two accounts a transfer touches, or a payment and its refunds. Tagging by shop is the classic mistake. A shop with 40% of the traffic then puts 40% of the load on one slot, so on one node, and adding nodes won't help.

Keys that change together share a tag. Make the tag as narrow as the change.

Slots move: to add a node, to empty one, to even out the load. The classic way marks the slot MIGRATING on the old node and IMPORTING on the new one, then copies its keys over in batches with MIGRATE. Meanwhile the old node still serves the keys it has. For a key it no longer has, it answers ASK 9055 127.0.0.1:7003: send this one command there, after an ASKING command, but leave your table alone, since the slot hasn't finished moving. A command whose keys are split between the two nodes gets TRYAGAIN. Redis 8.4 added atomic slot migration: CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT on the new node copies the whole slot, its keys as they were at one moment plus the writes that arrive meanwhile, then switches the owner in one step. In the lab it moved 1,001 keys in 31 ms with no pause in writes.

A cluster also does the job of Sentinel, the watcher programs from Persistence and replication that promote a replica when its primary dies. Give each primary a replica. When a primary is unreachable for cluster-node-timeout, the other primaries vote, and its replica takes over its slots. Sentinel protects one primary that holds everything; a cluster splits the data and fails over each part on its own.

Splitting the keys solves the size problem. It doesn't stop one command from slowing everyone down, and that's next.

sections.h: When every client slows down at once, find the one slow command
sections.html:
The pattern looks like this. Every program that uses one Redis gets slow answers at the same moment: the slowest one in a hundred goes from 1 ms to 300 ms. Yet the processor graph of the Redis machine stays calm. Inside an in-memory store explains it. One thread runs every command, so one slow command delays everything queued behind it, whatever key it touches. And one busy core on a 16-core machine (a core runs one thread at a time) barely moves the graph.

KEYS is the classic culprit. It lists every key that matches a pattern, in one command. In the lab, KEYS demo:l10:refund:* matched nothing and still walked all 1,000,000 keys: 150 to 340 ms, and a GET sent meanwhile from another thread waited as long. SCAN does the same walk in slices. Each call visits roughly COUNT entries of the key table and returns a cursor, a bookmark for the next call, so other clients are served in between. A full SCAN with COUNT 1000 took 1,000 calls and about 2 seconds in all, yet the slowest GET during it waited 16 to 27 ms on the same machine. The price is weaker promises: SCAN can return a key twice, and a key added during the walk may or may not appear.

The same reasoning covers every command whose cost grows with the size of a key. Commands that read a whole hash, set or list at once, such as HGETALL, SMEMBERS or LRANGE 0 -1, are slow on a big key (read it in pages with HSCAN, SSCAN or ranges). So is DEL of a big key (UNLINK frees it on a background thread instead), and so is a long Lua script.

One slow command makes every client slow. Find that command before you blame the network.

Redis keeps the evidence. The slow log holds the last 128 commands that ran longer than slowlog-log-slower-than, 10,000 microseconds (10 ms) by default. It times only the work on the command thread, never the network or the wait in the queue. In the lab, SLOWLOG GET showed KEYS demo:l10:refund:* at 145,531 microseconds.

The latency monitor (off by default; CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 10 turns it on) records slow events that aren't commands. One is the fork for a background save from Persistence and replication. Others are a write to the disk that took too long (an fsync() call), or a long run of deleting expired keys (Expiry, eviction and memory). LATENCY DOCTOR turns them into advice. INFO commandstats gives calls and microseconds per call for each command. It catches the case where no single command is slow, but one runs a million times a minute.

When none of those shows anything, measure the machine. redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 100 measures how long the operating system keeps the Redis process from running at all. On the lab's Docker virtual machine, shared with other programs, the worst stall was about 50 ms: no command was slow, and still some replies waited that long.

Commands aren't the only thing that can grow too big. Next, we'll find the keys that do.

code.title: LatencyDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l10.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.CommandArguments; import redis.clients.jedis.DefaultJedisClientConfig; import redis.clients.jedis.Protocol; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.params.ScanParams; import redis.clients.jedis.resps.ScanResult; import redis.clients.jedis.resps.Slowlog; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * Loads 1,000,000 payments, then looks for refund keys twice while a second client sends GETs back to back: * once with KEYS (one command walks the whole keyspace) and once with SCAN (a thousand small steps). * Prints the slowest GET during each, the slow log's top entry, then deletes its keys. */ public class LatencyDemo { static final String PREFIX = "demo:l10:payment:"; static final String FILL = """ for i = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]) do redis.call('SET', KEYS[1] .. i, 'settled') end return 1 """; static final String CLEAN = """ for i = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]) do redis.call('UNLINK', KEYS[1] .. i) end return 1 """; static final int N = 1_000_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // a busy server can take more than the default 2 s to answer: wait up to 30 s try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379) .clientConfig(DefaultJedisClientConfig.builder().socketTimeoutMillis(30_000).build()).build()) { for (int from = 1; from <= N; from += 100_000) { redis.eval(FILL, 1, PREFIX, String.valueOf(from), String.valueOf(from + 99_999)); } redis.slowlogReset(); System.out.printf("loaded %,d payments; %,d keys in the database%n", N, redis.dbSize()); long[] keys = whileReading(redis, () -> redis.keys("demo:l10:refund:*")); System.out.printf("KEYS: 1 command, %,5d ms in all; the slowest GET meanwhile waited %,4d ms%n", keys[0], keys[1]); AtomicLong calls = new AtomicLong(); long[] scan = whileReading(redis, () -> { ScanParams match = new ScanParams().match("demo:l10:refund:*").count(1_000); String cursor = ScanParams.SCAN_POINTER_START; do { ScanResult<String> page = redis.scan(cursor, match); calls.incrementAndGet(); cursor = page.getCursor(); } while (!cursor.equals(ScanParams.SCAN_POINTER_START)); }); System.out.printf("SCAN: %,d commands, %,5d ms in all; the slowest GET meanwhile waited %,4d ms%n", calls.get(), scan[0], scan[1]); @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") List<Slowlog> log = Slowlog.from((List<Object>) redis.executeCommand(new CommandArguments(Protocol.Command.SLOWLOG).add("GET").add(128))); Slowlog top = log.stream().max((a, b) -> Long.compare(a.getExecutionTime(), b.getExecutionTime())).orElseThrow(); System.out.printf("entries in the slow log: %d; the slowest: %s, %,d microseconds%n", log.size(), top.getArgs(), top.getExecutionTime()); for (int from = 1; from <= N; from += 100_000) { redis.eval(CLEAN, 1, PREFIX, String.valueOf(from), String.valueOf(from + 99_999)); } } } /** Runs {@code task} while a second thread sends GETs back to back; returns {task ms, slowest GET in ms}. */ static long[] whileReading(RedisClient redis, Runnable task) throws InterruptedException { AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(true); AtomicLong slowestNanos = new AtomicLong(); Thread reader = new Thread(() -> { while (running.get()) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); redis.get(PREFIX + 42); slowestNanos.accumulateAndGet(System.nanoTime() - t0, Math::max); } }); reader.start(); Thread.sleep(200); slowestNanos.set(0); // only count what happens during the task long t0 = System.nanoTime(); task.run(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; running.set(false); reader.join(); return new long[] {ms, slowestNanos.get() / 1_000_000}; } }

the slowest: ${top.args}, %,d microseconds".format(top.executionTime)) for (from in 1..N step 100_000) redis.eval(CLEAN, 1, PREFIX, "$from", "${from + 99_999}") } } /** Runs [task] while a second thread sends GETs back to back; returns the task's ms and the slowest GET's ms. */ private fun RedisClient.whileReading(task: () -> Unit): Pair<Long, Long> { val running = AtomicBoolean(true) val slowestNanos = AtomicLong() val reader = thread { while (running.get()) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() get("${PREFIX}42") slowestNanos.accumulateAndGet(System.nanoTime() - t0) { a, b -> maxOf(a, b) } } } Thread.sleep(200) slowestNanos.set(0) // only count what happens during the task val t0 = System.nanoTime() task() val millis = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 running.set(false) reader.join() return millis to slowestNanos.get() / 1_000_000 }

try.expect: In the runs for this lesson, KEYS took 138 to 343 ms, and the slowest GET meanwhile waited 134 to 294 ms: it sat behind that one command. The SCAN loop took 1,000 commands and 0.8 to 2 seconds in all (13 seconds in one run while Docker's virtual machine was busy), and in quiet runs the slowest GET waited 10 to 27 ms. The demo's slow log line reads entries in the slow log: 1; the slowest: [KEYS, demo:l10:refund:*], 133,736 microseconds; in the busy run it counted 61 entries, because even small SCAN calls looked slow when the machine stalled. SLOWLOG GET 2 at the prompt shows the demo's clean-up instead: two EVAL entries of 122,344 and 138,812 microseconds, each deleting 100,000 keys in one script, with the script, its arguments and the client's address. A clean-up can be the slow command too. --intrinsic-latency 5 ends with a line like Worst run took 549284x longer than the average latency.: about 50 ms during which Docker's virtual machine didn't run Redis at all.

sections.h: Big keys, hot keys, and memory that doesn't come back
sections.html:
Two kinds of key cause most of the remaining trouble, and both defeat the cluster's plan of spreading the work over slots.

A big key is one key that grew. Picture a shop's hash, a key that holds many named fields like a small table, with 200,000 payments in it: 9.6 MB in one key. Every command that reads all of it is slow. It sits on one node however large the cluster is, and moving its slot means copying it in one piece. redis-cli --bigkeys walks the keys with SCAN and reports the biggest key of each type by number of elements; --memkeys reports bytes. The fix comes from Core data types and their encodings: split the key, by day or by a hash of the payment's id.

A hot key gets a large share of the traffic, such as the profile of the busiest shop, read on every payment. It lives in one slot, so one node's thread serves all of it, and adding nodes changes nothing. In the cloakroom, it's the one hook everyone asks for. Redis 8.6 added HOTKEYS to find them: HOTKEYS START METRICS 2 CPU NET records which keys use the most command-thread time and network bytes, and HOTKEYS GET reports them. In the lab, one shop profile took 35,266 of 42,732 microseconds of command time (83%) and 4.25 of 5.15 MB of traffic. The fixes: keep a copy inside each program (the client-side caching of Caching patterns and stampedes), read it from replicas, or split a hot counter into several keys and add them up.

Memory has its own trap. used_memory is what Redis's allocator, the code that hands out memory inside a program, has given to values. used_memory_rss is the process's RSS: the memory the kernel, the core of the operating system, has given it. Delete half your keys and the first drops while the second barely moves. The allocator keeps the freed pieces inside pages, the 4 KB blocks the kernel hands out, that still hold live values, and it can't return a page until all of it is free. Memory allocation: malloc, arenas and why RSS grows, in the Operating systems track, showed why. In the lab, 500,000 values of 100 bytes used 85 MB with an RSS of 101 MB. After deleting every other key: 50 MB used, RSS still 101 MB, a mem_fragmentation_ratio of 2.04. CONFIG SET activedefrag yes makes Redis move live values into fuller pages, a little at a time on the main thread. About 20 seconds later, RSS was 70 MB and the ratio 1.42. On a nearly empty server the ratio means nothing, because a few fixed megabytes dominate it.

The last choice is which Redis to run. Up to version 7.2, Redis came under the BSD license, which lets anyone use and change it. 7.4 moved to RSALv2 or SSPLv1, licenses that limit how others may offer it as a service, and 8.0 added AGPLv3, an open-source license, as a third choice. In March 2024 the Linux Foundation, a non-profit group, started Valkey from Redis 7.2.4 under BSD, backed by big companies such as Amazon and Google; it's now at 9.1. Everything in this track up to Redis 7.2 works on both. Newer commands differ: DELEX, INCREX, HOTKEYS, CLUSTER MIGRATION and BACKUP are Redis 8, while Valkey 9.0 has its own atomic slot migration and allows numbered databases in cluster mode. Choose by the license your company accepts, the managed service (a Redis that a cloud company runs for you) you'd rent, and which of those commands you need.

try.title: Find a big key and a hot key
steps: At a prompt on the single server (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), build a big hash and a shop profile, start HOTKEYS, and leave the prompt open.

From a second terminal in the labs folder, make one key hot and spread some other reads: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -n 50000 GET merchant:7:profile, then the same with -n 20000 -r 300 GET payment:__rand_int__. redis-benchmark is a tool that comes with Redis and sends a command many times. Back at the prompt, stop HOTKEYS and read the report.

Quit the prompt and run docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli --bigkeys, then --memkeys in place of --bigkeys. Finish with DEL merchant:7:payments merchant:7:profile, or docker compose -f env/redis.yml down -v if you're done with the track.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
EVAL "for i=1,200000 do redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'p'..i, '1250') end return redis.call('HLEN', KEYS[1])" 1 merchant:7:payments
MEMORY USAGE merchant:7:payments
SET merchant:7:profile '{"name":"Blue Fern Coffee","mcc":"5814"}'
HOTKEYS START METRICS 2 CPU NET
# run the two redis-benchmark commands from the second terminal
HOTKEYS STOP
HOTKEYS GET

try.expect: The EVAL prints (integer) 200000 and MEMORY USAGE about (integer) 9634717: 9.6 MB in one key. The benchmarks print lines like GET merchant:7:profile: 24875.62 requests per second, p50=0.911 msec (p50 is the time within which half the requests finished). HOTKEYS GET (trimmed) shows all-commands-all-slots-us 42732 and total-net-bytes 5150000. Under by-cpu-time-us comes first "merchant:7:profile" 35266, far ahead of keys like "payment:000000000022" 489 (redis-benchmark pads the random numbers), and under by-net-bytes "merchant:7:profile" 4250000. Your numbers differ; the order doesn't. --bigkeys ends with Biggest hash found "merchant:7:payments" has 200000 fields and Biggest string found "merchant:7:profile" has 40 bytes; --memkeys reports the same hash as 9634717 bytes. Both walk the keys with SCAN, so they're safe on a busy server.

opening:
Picture a café at the morning rush with one till. The cashier is quick, but serves one customer at a time, and the queue reaches the door. Someone copying every sale into a spare book keeps the records safe, but the queue doesn't move.

The payments program has the same problem. It keeps its notes, counters and saved answers in Redis, a program that holds data in a computer's memory and answers very fast. They've grown to 40 GB and 300,000 commands a second, and Redis works through every command one at a time.

The fix looks easy: more tills, and each customer sent to one. But the first way most people choose sends almost everyone to a different till the day one more opens. And a family paying together needs one till.

Persistence and replication copied Redis, and copies don't make it bigger. In this lesson, we'll split the keys over three servers, find the right one for each command, and hunt what holds everyone up. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with one till and a queue to the door. Splitting the keys into 16,384 slots gave each primary its own share of the queue. Hash tags kept a family's keys at one till, and the slow log found the one command that held everyone up.

On the lab's Redis, or any Redis you can reach, run INFO commandstats and find the command with the most time in total.

That ends the Caching track. Next, in Encoding, APIs and workflows, we'll follow data as it leaves a program: how does an object in memory become bytes that another program, perhaps in another language, can read?

compare.title: One payment's keys through a cluster client, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: ClusterWrites.java (Jedis)
java.html: static final String SETTLE = "redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2])"; try (RedisClusterClient cluster = RedisClusterClient.builder() .nodes(Set.of(new HostAndPort("127.0.0.1", 7001))) // one seed node is enough .build()) { cluster.set("{payment:p-981}:status", "approved"); // routed to slot 445's owner cluster.incr("{payment:p-981}:attempts"); // same tag, same slot, same node // one atomic step over both keys: a script, since the cluster client has no MULTI Object deleted = cluster.eval(SETTLE, List.of("{payment:p-981}:status", "{payment:p-981}:attempts"), List.of("settled")); }

kotlin.title: ClusterWrites.kt (Lettuce coroutines)
kotlin.html: const val SETTLE = "redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[2])" val client = RedisClusterClient.create("redis://127.0.0.1:7001") // Lettuce; one seed node is enough client.connect().use { connection -> val redis = connection.coroutines() runBlocking { redis.set("{payment:p-981}:status", "approved") // routed to slot 445's owner redis.incr("{payment:p-981}:attempts") // same tag, same slot, same node // one atomic step over both keys: a script, since the cluster API has no MULTI val deleted = redis.eval<Long>(SETTLE, ScriptOutputType.INTEGER, arrayOf("{payment:p-981}:status", "{payment:p-981}:attempts"), "settled") } } client.shutdown()

compare.note: Both clients start from one seed node, the one address you give them, then load the slot table and route every command by slot. {payment:p-981} hashes to slot 445, so all of that payment's keys live on one node, and a script over them runs there as one step: both versions printed 1 (one key deleted) against the lab cluster. Neither client gives you MULTI on a cluster connection. Jedis 8's RedisClusterClient.multi() throws UnsupportedOperationException, and Lettuce's cluster API has no multi at all. With Lettuce you can take one node's connection from client.partitions and run MULTI there, but a script over tagged keys works everywhere. Jedis blocks the calling thread for each call. The Kotlin version suspends the coroutine instead, a Kotlin task that can pause without holding a thread, and shares one connection per node among all callers.

worked.title: Move a two-key Lua script onto a cluster

steps.say: This small Lua script takes money from one account and adds it to another in one step; the Transactions track's lesson on serial execution builds scripts like it in full. On the lab cluster, with keys named the old way, it fails before it runs, because the two keys are in different slots.
steps.code:
127.0.0.1:7001> EVAL "local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) return 1" 2 acct:a acct:b 3000
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

steps.say: Tag by the unit that must change in one step. A transfer between one customer's own accounts touches only that customer, so {customer:991} goes in both names. Check that the slots match, then run the same script: it moves 3,000 out of 10,000.
steps.code:
127.0.0.1:7001> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {customer:991}:main
(integer) 5094
127.0.0.1:7001> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {customer:991}:savings
(integer) 5094
127.0.0.1:7001> SET {customer:991}:main 10000
OK
127.0.0.1:7001> EVAL "...the same script..." 2 {customer:991}:main {customer:991}:savings 3000
(integer) 1
127.0.0.1:7001> MGET {customer:991}:main {customer:991}:savings
1) "7000"
2) "3000"

steps.say: In code, the cluster client routes the EVAL by its keys, so nothing else changes. One function builds the key names, so no caller can forget the tag.
steps.code: static String account(long customerId, String name) { return "{customer:" + customerId + "}:" + name; // one tag per customer: one slot } Object moved = cluster.eval(TRANSFER_SCRIPT, List.of(account(991, "main"), account(991, "savings")), List.of("3000"));

alt.html: fun account(customerId: Long, name: String) = "{customer:$customerId}:$name" // one tag per customer: one slot val moved = cluster.eval(TRANSFER_SCRIPT, listOf(account(991, "main"), account(991, "savings")), listOf("3000"))

steps.say: A transfer between two customers has no shared tag that wouldn't put everyone in one slot. So make it two single-slot steps, each safe to repeat, keyed by the transfer's id as in Rate limiting and idempotency keys. Take the money from customer 991 and record t-77 in that customer's slot. Then add it to customer 412 and record t-77 in theirs, retrying each step until it reports done. If the money must never be missing from both accounts, even for a moment, keep that transfer in a database and use Redis only for the fast checks around it.
steps.code:
debit  {customer:991}:main  by 3000 unless {customer:991}:done:t-77 exists   (one script, one slot)
credit {customer:412}:main  by 3000 unless {customer:412}:done:t-77 exists   (one script, another slot)

lab.title: Route keys like a cluster client, then find the slow command and the big key
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 17 fail: 11 in ClusterRouterTest, which needs no Docker because ModelCluster.kt (done for you) is a three-node cluster in memory, and 6 in DiagnosticsTest, which use the shared Redis container.

In ClusterRouter.kt, write HashSlots.crc16, hashTag and slot. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l10.ClusterRouterTest': the four slot tests pass. The numbers in slots match what a real Redis 8 cluster answered come from this lesson's Try its.
Read ModelCluster.send: it's how a real node chooses between running a command, MOVED, ASK, CROSSSLOT and TRYAGAIN. Then write ClusterRouter.execute and run the class again until all 11 pass.
In Diagnostics.java, write slowest (sort the slow log by time spent) and biggestKeys (SCAN with MATCH, then MEMORY USAGE for each key). Run all 17 tests.
hints: CRC16, byte by byte: crc = crc xor ((b.toInt() and 0xFF) shl 8), then 8 times crc = if (crc and 0x8000 != 0) (crc shl 1) xor 0x1021 else crc shl 1, then crc = crc and 0xFFFF.
hashTag: val open = key.indexOf('{'), then key.indexOf('}', open + 1). Use the whole key if either is -1 or if the close comes right after the open.
In execute, keep node and asking in two vars and loop with repeat(maxRedirects + 1). A return inside works, because repeat is inline.
In biggestKeys, keep a Set of keys you have seen, sort with Comparator.comparingLong(BigKey::bytes).reversed(), and return at most n.

drill.title: Slot math from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write hashTag(key) and slot(key) from memory; you may call a crc16(bytes) that you don't write. Then, without running anything, say which of these share a slot: {merchant:7}:payments, merchant:7, {merchant:7, x{merchant:7}y.

answer.html: static String hashTag(String key) { int open = key.indexOf('{'); if (open < 0) return key; int close = key.indexOf('}', open + 1); if (close < 0 || close == open + 1) return key; // no }, or {} with nothing inside return key.substring(open + 1, close); } static int slot(String key) { return crc16(hashTag(key).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) % 16_384; } // {merchant:7}:payments, merchant:7 and x{merchant:7}y all hash "merchant:7": slot 10890. // {merchant:7 has no closing brace, so the whole key is hashed: slot 2924.

alt.html: fun hashTag(key: String): String { val open = key.indexOf('{') if (open < 0) return key val close = key.indexOf('}', open + 1) if (close < 0 || close == open + 1) return key // no }, or {} with nothing inside return key.substring(open + 1, close) } fun slot(key: String): Int = crc16(hashTag(key).toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)) % 16_384 // {merchant:7}:payments, merchant:7 and x{merchant:7}y all hash "merchant:7": slot 10890. // {merchant:7 has no closing brace, so the whole key is hashed: slot 2924.

recap: Redis Cluster spreads keys over 16,384 slots: slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each slot belongs to one primary. Adding a fourth node moves only the slots it takes, 25% of the keys, against 75% with hash mod N.

A node that doesn't own a key's slot answers MOVED <slot> <address> and never passes the command on. Cluster-aware clients keep the slot table, route each command themselves and reload the table on MOVED.

Commands with several keys, transactions and scripts need all their keys in one slot, or the node answers CROSSSLOT. A hash tag {...} hashes only the tagged part; tag by the smallest unit that must change in one step.
While a slot moves the classic way, ASK sends one command to the new node after ASKING and leaves the table alone. Redis 8.4's CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT moves a whole slot in one step.
When every client slows down at once, look for one slow command: the slow log, the latency monitor, INFO commandstats, then --intrinsic-latency. Use SCAN instead of KEYS, and UNLINK for big keys.
The limit: slots spread keys, not load. A big key or a hot key stays on one node however many you add, so find them with --bigkeys, --memkeys and HOTKEYS (8.6), and split them.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate how a cluster-aware client finds the node for GET {payment:p-981}:status, what happens when a slot has moved since the client started, and why the braces are in the key name.
explain.answer: The client works out the slot itself. Because the name has braces with something inside, only payment:p-981 is hashed: its CRC16, mod 16,384, is slot 445. When the client started, it loaded the slot table from a node, so it looks up slot 445, finds the primary that owns it, and sends the GET straight there over its connection to that node. Nodes never pass commands on. If someone moved slot 445 since then, the old owner answers MOVED 445 with the new address. The client tries again there and fixes its table, usually by reloading all of it, so later commands go straight to the new owner. If the slot is in the middle of a move, the old owner may answer ASK instead, for keys it no longer has. Then the client sends only that one command to the new node, after ASKING, and leaves its table alone. The braces are there so that every key of this payment, its status, its attempts counter and its refunds, lands in the same slot. Then one MULTI or one Lua script can change them together, which a cluster refuses with CROSSSLOT when keys are in different slots. We tag by payment, not by shop, so that one big shop doesn't pile all its traffic onto one slot and one node.

deeper.html:
Reading from replicas. A cluster replica redirects every command to its primary unless the connection sends READONLY first. Then it serves reads for its primary's slots, a little behind, as Persistence and replication explained. Both Jedis and Lettuce can route reads to replicas (Lettuce's ReadFrom setting), which spreads a hot key's reads over more threads.

Per-slot numbers. Redis 8.4 added CLUSTER SLOT-STATS, which reports per slot how many keys it holds and how much processor time and network traffic it used. It answers the question HOTKEYS answers for keys, one level up: which slot, and so which hash tag, is too hot.

Pub/sub on a cluster. Pub/sub is Redis's way of sending a message to every program listening on a named channel. A plain PUBLISH is copied to every node in the cluster, because a listener can be connected anywhere. Sharded pub/sub (SPUBLISH, SSUBSCRIBE, Redis 7.0) assigns each channel to a slot like a key, so a message travels only to the nodes that serve that slot. On a cluster, messages meant for many programs at once belong there.

One database only. Redis Cluster supports only database 0, so SELECT 1 fails; separate data with key prefixes or separate clusters. Valkey 9.0 lifted that limit for its own cluster mode.

Write safety in a split. The cluster spec is open about losses: replication is asynchronous, so a primary can acknowledge a write and fail before its replica has it, and a primary cut off on the smaller side of a network split keeps taking writes until cluster-node-timeout passes, then refuses them. Writes made there in that window are lost when the majority side promotes its replica. That's the failover story from Persistence and replication again, once per primary.

Valkey in practice. Valkey publishes the Docker image (the package Docker starts a container from) valkey/valkey, and its CLI is valkey-cli, which accepts the same commands. The two have changed separately since 2024, so treat a move between them as a migration: test it with your own data and commands rather than assume a file copied from one loads in the other.

The general picture. Redis Cluster is one point in a larger design space: a fixed number of hash slots, assigned by hand or by a tool, with clients that route by a cached table. The Partitioning track compares it with key-range splits, consistent hashing, automatic rebalancing and routing tiers, and its lessons on Cassandra, MongoDB and DynamoDB show the same questions answered differently.
